title: FDA clears DeepHealth's AI breast ultrasound for autonomous lesion detection
subtitle: The 510(k) clearance covers automated lesion detection, characterization and reporting from ultrasound imaging, and follows a multi-reader multi-case study with 16 US board-certified radiologists.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The FDA granted 510(k) clearance on July 30 to DeepHealth Breast Ultrasound, an AI-powered imaging tool from DeepHealth, a wholly owned subsidiary of RadNet. The system automates three linked tasks — lesion detection, lesion characterization, and structured reporting — in a single workflow that previously required manual attention from a sonographer and a reviewing radiologist. Validation came through a multi-reader, multi-case study involving 16 US board-certified radiologists, followed by validation in live clinical settings. The product is commercially available in the United States as of clearance, and customers can pursue reimbursement under an existing Category III CPT code for quantitative ultrasound tissue characterization.

The reason this clearance matters is scope. FDA-authorized AI in radiology is now a large category — the agency's device list crossed 1,000 entries earlier this year — but most clearances cover mammography, where the imaging modality is standardized and lesions have well-characterized visual signatures. Ultrasound is harder: operator technique matters, image quality varies, and the lesion-detection task is inherently more ambiguous. Clearing an AI system to do detection plus characterization plus reporting on ultrasound is a step up in scope from what most previously cleared tools were allowed to do.

Set against the broader healthcare AI arc, this is one of three material FDA moves in the last two weeks: Corvista's cleared PCWP tool for heart failure (July 29), CliniComp's PACS viewer with native AI (July 7), and now DeepHealth Breast Ultrasound. The pattern is consistent — the agency is granting clearances to systems that perform previously human-only interpretive tasks, but only under a 510(k) predicate-device standard rather than the more stringent De Novo or PMA pathway. That keeps velocity high and risk contained, at the cost of not yet establishing a clear regulatory frame for genuinely novel AI capabilities.

For learners: if you are studying AI in healthcare, the Category III CPT code question is where the practical action is. FDA clearance means an AI tool can be sold; a CPT code means providers can bill insurers for using it. DeepHealth is using an existing Category III code — Category III codes are temporary, five-year designations for emerging technology, with no guaranteed payment amount. The unresolved question for the whole field is when AI-assisted radiology gets its own permanent Category I code with defined reimbursement. Watch for CMS movement on that in 2027; it will determine which of these cleared tools become standard of care and which stay pilots.
